title: Forget Teslas: Africa’s EV boom is happening elsewhere, but we have a problem
body:
We might be thinking about EVs in Africa all wrong.

While the global conversation is obsessed with electric cars, the real transformation on the African continent is happening elsewhere.

And honestly—that’s where the story gets interesting.

East Africa is quickly emerging as a serious EV hub on the continent.

Countries like Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda are leading the change through policy, pilots, and early adoption (see the figure attached).

But here’s what stands out most to me. The transition isn’t driven by private cars like in Europe or the US. It’s being driven by motorcycles and 3-wheelers—the true backbone of daily mobility in this region. This is a complete system redesign and that’s why this moment feels bigger than just “EV adoption.”

This feels like a classic leapfrog moment. Africa has the chance to skip the legacy systems and build something more suited to its reality.

But here’s a hard truth we can’t ignore: electricity remains a greatest challenge.

More than 600 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack reliable access to power. Even those with access suffer from unstable power supply. Without solving this, the idea of scaling e-mobility (no matter the vehicle type) hits a ceiling.

Companies like Roam and Ampersand are building parallel infrastructure models to work around electricity-related constraints, among others. Though impressive and necessary, this raises a critical question: Can fragmented, niche solutions really support a continent-wide transition? It also raises localization challenge.

If Africa is going to unlock the full potential of e-mobility, it will take more than isolated innovation. It requires national, system-level solutions: integrated power, transport, and policy working together at scale.

**Bottom Line:** If e-mobility is already taking shape on the continent despite its electricity constraints, addressing this challenge will redefine the global EV playbook.

Why? Africa’s e-mobility transition isn’t about luxury vehicles or early adopters. It is about mass, everyday mobility at scale. So, if it wins here; it wins big.
